title: Red flags in a ledger
learn: How to check an extract is complete before you test it
Four red-flag tests, and the rows that only look wrong
Why a red flag only tells you where to look
do: Tie a 500-entry payment register, then run four tests on it
Decide what the flags show, and what they don’t
Write the note to your lead

case.role: First-year article assistant, lent to the forensic desk for the week
case.client: Khamang Foods Private Limited, a Ranjangaon company that makes namkeen and chikki. Our firm is its internal auditor; this review is separate and confidential.
case.team: Manav Bhatia (forensic lead) and you; Ashwin Pradhan, the CFO, is the only contact at Khamang
case.goal: Run four red-flag tests on eleven months of payments from Khamang’s plant account, and give Manav a clean list of leads before the purchase and accounts desks hear a word of it.
case.where: Review room, our Prabhat Road office · Thursday 4 March 2027

messages: Confidential one. Khamang’s MD got an unsigned letter about the purchase desk. Before anyone is asked anything, run my four tests on their plant account’s payments. Rules are in my note.
Leads, not conclusions. List and a short note to me by 5. Not a word to anyone at Khamang.

documents.title: Manav’s note · the four tests
documents.subject: Khamang Foods: payments from the plant account
body: On 1 March Khamang’s Managing Director got an unsigned letter saying someone on the purchase desk is buying from a supplier that never delivers. He wants the payments looked at before anyone is asked anything. Ashwin Pradhan, the CFO, is our only contact.
## Scope
Every entry in the plant account’s payment register, 1 April 2026 to 28 February 2027, as Ashwin exported it on 3 March. Tie it to his ledger totals before you test anything, and work on a copy.
## The four tests
- **Duplicate:** the same vendor, the same bill number once spaces, “/” and “-” are taken out, and the same amount. Flag the later payment only.
- **Round sum:** an exact multiple of ₹10,000 with no bill, PO or agreement number in the Bill / ref column.
- **Office closed:** posted on a Saturday, a Sunday or a holiday in the accounts office calendar, by a person. AUTOBANK is the bank feed, not a person.
- **Vendor–employee match:** the vendor’s PAN, bank account or address is the same as an employee’s in the employee master. Flag every payment to that vendor.
One flag per payment, with the test it fails.
## How we work
A red flag is a lead, not a finding. Write what the papers show, not what you think happened. Talk to nobody at Khamang about any of this; questions come to me.

documents.title: Ashwin’s mail · the export
documents.subject: Plant account: payment register, 1 April to 28 February
body: Manav,
Attached, run from my login this afternoon:
- the bank payment register for our Narmada Valley Bank current account ending 3381, 01-04-2026 to 28-02-2027, no filter: 500 entries, ₹14,64,39,709.12;
- the ledger totals for the same account and period, party by party;
- the vendor master for the 17 vendors paid from the account, and HR’s employee master for staff with ERP roles;
- our accounts office calendar.

Shikrapur’s bank account was put back to its verified one on 18 November, after your internal audit team’s call-back. The bank is tracing the two September payments to the changed account, so they are outside this review.
This is the plant account: we pay the Ranjangaon plant’s local suppliers from it. Salaries, taxes and the head-office suppliers go from our Pune accounts.
Jyoti also keeps the net-banking batch reports for the Friday runs. For the same period they come to 443 payments, ₹13,26,93,859.17. I can send those too.
Jyoti thinks all this is for the internal audit’s year-end file.
Ashwin

tasks.title: Tie the export before you test it
tasks.prompt: Before any test, make sure the register is complete and settle how you will handle it. Read Ashwin’s mail, the register’s total row and notes, and his ledger totals.
hints: Put the register’s count and total next to the ledger totals print, and read how Ashwin ran the export.

questions.text: What tells you the register is complete enough to test?

options.text: Jyoti’s batch reports: 443 payments, ₹13,26,93,859.17, every Friday run released by Jyoti and authorised by Ashwin.
options.why: The batch reports hold only the Friday runs. The one-off NEFTs, the RTGS payments and the bank’s own debits sit outside them: test only those reports and nine of this register’s nineteen leads never show up.

options.text: Every one of the 17 vendors in the vendor master appears in the register at least once, so no vendor’s payments have been left out.
options.why: Every vendor can appear and payments can still be missing. Completeness is a count and a total agreed to another record.

options.text: Its 500 entries and ₹14,64,39,709.12 agree to the ledger totals for the same account and period, and Ashwin ran it with no filter.
options.why: Count and total agree to a second record for the whole period, run with no filter: now a test that finds nothing means something. Both prints come from one ERP; if I need more, the bank’s statement is the next tie.

options.text: Ashwin, the CFO, ran it from his own login and sent it himself, which is enough to rely on.
options.why: Who sent it tells you nothing about what is in it. Check the file, not the sender.

questions.text: Ashwin offers to have Jyoti tidy the register first: drop the bank charges and join each part payment to its balance. What do you say?

options.text: Yes to both: the bank charges are not vendor payments, and a part payment and its balance are one bill, so joining them saves you work.
options.why: Then the file is no longer what the ERP produced, and Jyoti would learn what we are testing.

options.text: No. Keep the export as it came and work on a copy: an edited file is no longer evidence, and the tidy-up would tip Jyoti off.
options.why: The export as it came out of the ERP is the evidence. Every judgement on it is yours, made on a copy, where I can see it.

options.text: Yes, but only the bank charges: the bank feed posts them, so none of the four tests can need them.
options.why: Drop them and the register no longer ties to the ledger totals, which count the 17 bank charges too. The file stays as the ERP produced it.

options.text: No, but ask Jyoti to mark the entries she thinks are odd, so that the tests start from her list and nothing she knows about is missed.
options.why: That tells the accounts desk what we are doing, and puts her judgement where the tests should be.

tasks.title: Run the four tests on the register
tasks.prompt: Run Manav’s four tests on all 500 entries. The buttons narrow the list; the rule in his note decides. Flag each payment that fails a test, with its reason: one flag per payment. Your flags go to Manav when you move on.
hints: The Weekend button knows Saturdays and Sundays, not Khamang’s holidays: search each date in the calendar. Leave AUTOBANK’s entries alone.
A duplicate is the same vendor, bill and amount: flag only the second payment. The same amount with a new bill number every month is a monthly bill.

lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change them after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Manav. You can read your flags but not change them.

tasks.title: What the flags mean
tasks.prompt: Manav has your list. At his request Ashwin has pulled the ERP trail for Pranjal’s bills: it is the new paper in your documents. Three questions before you write the note.
hints: Keep what the papers show apart from what it might mean. Then compare Pranjal’s rows in the trail with the three other vendors’ rows.

questions.text: Pranjal Packaging’s bank account is Yogesh Narwade’s salary account, and its address is Mahendra Kharat’s home. What goes in your note to Manav?

options.text: That Yogesh and Mahendra are taking money through a vendor they set up, and should be suspended today.
options.why: That is a conclusion, and a suspension is management’s call, on my advice. Write what the masters show.

options.text: That Pranjal’s bank account and address match two employees’ records, its eight payments listed, and no view on why.
options.why: The facts and where they came from, with the payments they touch. A relative, an old account or a typing slip could still explain a match.

options.text: Nothing yet: a match can be a typing slip, so check it quietly with Yogesh before it goes on paper.
options.why: Asking Yogesh tells one of the two people the match points to. The match comes to me as it stands.

options.text: That Pranjal is a fictitious vendor, so its eight payments, ₹3,90,000 in all, should be recovered from both men right away.
options.why: Nobody has shown yet that Pranjal supplied nothing. Recovery comes after the facts, not before them.

questions.text: Every Pranjal bill passed the three-way match: PO, GRN and bill agree. What does the trail add?

options.text: Nothing new: every bill has a PO and a GRN that agree with it, so the goods came in and the three-way match has done its job.
options.why: Agreeing papers prove only that the papers agree. Look at who made the GRNs, and what is missing from them.

options.text: Yogesh Narwade raised all eight POs, which shows he arranged every purchase from Pranjal himself.
options.why: Yogesh raises the POs for other vendors too: his name is on Shikrapur’s, Nhavare’s and Uruli’s rows. On its own it shows nothing.

options.text: Nitin Bhosale approved all eight POs on his phone, so the approval control failed and Nitin is the lead.
options.why: Nitin approves on his phone for other vendors too, as Nhavare’s row shows. Note it as a fact; it does not make him the lead.

options.text: Mahendra Kharat, who lives at Pranjal’s address, keyed in all eight GRNs; none has a QC check or gate entry, unlike the rest.
options.why: That is the fact to chase: the GRNs say goods came in and nothing else does. A three-way match proves little when the person behind one paper is linked to the vendor.

questions.text: Sachin Dhumal keeps Khamang’s stores; Lonand Masala’s proprietor is Sanjay Dhumal. Should Lonand’s payments be on your list?

options.text: Yes: a shared surname is enough to put Lonand beside Pranjal, whose proprietor shares Yogesh’s surname.
options.why: Pranjal is on the list for the bank account and the address, not the surname. Surnames repeat across whole talukas.

options.text: No: the test needs the same PAN, bank account or address, and Lonand shares none of them with any employee.
options.why: A surname alone is not a lead. If something else turns up later, Lonand comes back for a look.

options.text: Yes, but only the payments for the goods that Sachin’s stores received, since he could have passed a short delivery.
options.why: The test does not look at who received the goods, and nothing in the masters links Lonand to Sachin.

options.text: No: Lonand has supplied Khamang since 2022, long before the letter came.
options.why: Age does not clear a vendor. Lonand stays off the list because nothing links it, not because it is old.

tasks.title: Write the note to Manav
tasks.prompt: Manav wants one short note: what you ran, what the tests catch, what Pranjal’s papers show, what none of it proves yet, and what to pull next. Pick the right line for each part.
hints: Facts with their source, and counts that follow the rules in Manav’s note, whatever your list said. The next steps tell nobody at Khamang; who is asked what is Manav’s call.

freeText.label: Your own line for the note

options.text: I ran the four tests on the Friday batch reports for 1 April 2026 – 28 February 2027: 443 payments, ₹13,26,93,859.17, which hold every payment the plant account made.
options.why: The batch reports leave out every one-off payment, and the first payment of KEO/1184 was one of those.

options.text: I ran the four tests on the whole payment register for 1 April 2026 – 28 February 2027: 500 entries, ₹14,64,39,709.12, tied to the ledger totals first.
options.why: Scope, period and the tie-out in one line. I can rely on a test only when I know what it ran on.

options.text: I ran the four tests on the register after Jyoti took out the bank charges and joined the part payments, so it held only real vendor payments.
options.why: An edited file is not evidence, and the edit told the accounts desk what we were doing.

options.text: Nineteen payments fail a test: 8 to Pranjal Packaging Supplies, 3 bills paid twice, 4 round sums with nothing behind them and 4 entries staff posted on closed days.
options.why: Each count follows the rules in my note: only the second payment of a pair, and only postings by people on closed days.

options.text: Twenty-six payments fail a test: 8 to Pranjal Packaging Supplies, 6 duplicates (both payments of each pair), 4 round sums, and 8 weekend entries, the bank feed’s included.
options.why: The first payment of a pair is the right one and AUTOBANK is not a person, so the count is inflated; and the two holiday postings on weekdays are missing.

options.text: Fifteen payments fail a test: 8 to Pranjal Packaging Supplies, 3 bills paid a second time, 4 round sums, and no office-closed entries, as only the bank feed posted at weekends.
options.why: People posted twice at weekends and twice more on company holidays that fall on weekdays.

options.text: Pranjal’s proprietor shares Yogesh Narwade’s surname, a common one around Shirur, and its eight bills, ₹3,90,000 in all, each have a PO and a GRN behind them, so they need no more work.
options.why: The surname is the least of it. The bank account and the address are the match, and the GRNs are the problem.

options.text: Pranjal Packaging Supplies exists only on paper: Yogesh Narwade and Mahendra Kharat have taken all of its ₹3,90,000 between them and should be suspended today, before any of the records go missing.
options.why: That is a conclusion the papers do not reach yet, and it names two people as guilty in writing.

options.text: Pranjal’s bank account is Yogesh Narwade’s salary account; its address is Mahendra Kharat’s home. Mahendra keyed in the GRNs for all eight bills (₹3,90,000), none with a QC check or gate entry.
options.why: Facts, each with the paper it comes from: the masters for the links, the trail for the GRNs.

options.text: These are leads, not findings. Each could still have an innocent explanation until the papers rule it out, and I have told nobody at Khamang.
options.why: That is the line a lead’s note has to carry, and the reason the next step is mine to decide.

options.text: These are frauds on Khamang, and the three entries apexec02 posted while the office was shut show the accounts desk was hiding them.
options.why: A posting on a closed day is a reason to ask, not proof of hiding anything.

options.text: These are small and routine: duplicates and advances happen in every company, and Pranjal’s bills are under ₹50,000 each, so Khamang can sort them out itself.
options.why: Small is not harmless. Pranjal’s bills look kept under the three-quotation line on purpose, and a lead stays a lead whatever its size.

options.text: Next, I will phone Pranjal Packaging and visit its Karegaon address this week, to see for myself whether the business exists at all.
options.why: A call or a visit warns whoever is behind Pranjal. Site visits and interviews are for me to decide.

options.text: Next, I will ask Jyoti to stop Pranjal’s payments and recover the three duplicates, and tell Yogesh why we are asking, so that he can explain himself before we write anything down.
options.why: That tells the accounts desk and the person linked to the vendor before anyone has the papers.

options.text: Next, I suggest we pull Pranjal’s vendor-creation file, the stock issues of its material and the vendors’ statements for the duplicates. Who is asked what, and when, is your call.
options.why: Papers first, people later; who is asked what stays my decision.

wrap.text: Nineteen of the five hundred fail a test. Pranjal is the one I take to the MD tomorrow: a staff salary account, a staff home address, eight bills under the three-quotation line, no gate entry. The duplicates look like slips; Uruli, Nhavare and Kedgaon owe ₹16.1 lakh back either way.

wrapPartial.text: The holiday postings and the second payment of a pair are the easy ones to get wrong; check yours against my note before anything goes to the MD. In your note to me, write only what the papers show.

wrapRetry.text: One test at a time, in my note’s order: Duplicates, flagging only the second payment; then Round sums with nothing behind them; then Weekend and a search for each holiday in the calendar, people’s postings only; then Match masters, and every payment to the vendor it shows.

passNeeds.note: Your list needs more of the leads, each with the right reason, before this passes.

model.intro: Nineteen of the 500 entries fail a test: eight payments to Pranjal Packaging Supplies, the second payments of three bills, four round sums with nothing behind them and four entries staff posted while the office was shut. Everything else passes, the bank feed’s weekend and holiday charges included.

The first payment of each duplicate pair, and Kedgaon’s part payment and balance on KEO/0975.
Babhulsar’s ₹2,31,280 and Lonikand’s ₹35,400 every month: new bill numbers each time.

The Thursday batches of 30 April, 1 October and 24 December, moved a day early for Friday holidays.

blocks.text: The tests choose where to look; they never say what happened. Pranjal could still be a relative’s firm set up carelessly. Its vendor file and the stock records will tell us, not the match.

principles: Tie an extract to a second record before you test it. Work on a copy; the file you were given stays as it came.
Apply each rule as written: a bank-feed posting, a batch moved for a holiday or a monthly bill is not a hit.
A red flag picks out a payment for a closer look. The papers decide what it was.

interview.q: How did you find duplicate payments in 500 entries?
interview.checking: Whether you can define a duplicate before you hunt for one, and keep the false ones out.
outline: I grouped payments by vendor and amount, then compared bill numbers with spaces, slashes and hyphens stripped.
I flagged only the second payment of each pair[[: {dup} in the simulation]].
A monthly bill of the same amount with a new bill number is not a duplicate.

interview.q: A vendor’s bank account matches an employee’s. Is that fraud?
interview.checking: Whether you keep facts apart from conclusions, and know who decides what happens next.
outline: Not by itself. It is a red flag: a relative, an ex-employee or a typo could explain it.
I flagged that vendor’s payments[[, {match} in the simulation,]] and gave my lead both master entries.
